evidence: Caes. BG 6.34: magnam rēs dīligentiam requīrēbat (Lewis & Short)
Cic. Imp. Pomp. 64: virtūtēs animī magnae et multae requīruntur (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Of what a task or a situation calls for; in the passive, “to be required”.

terms.grammar: impersonal: the dative of the person, the thing needed in the ablative or the nominative
terms.gloss: there is need of; it is needed
evidence: Ter. Ad. 996: quid factō opus est
Cic. Fam. 9.25.3: opus est auctōritāte tuā (Lewis & Short s.v. opus)
Traupman p. 104: I (you, we) need money, opus est mihi (tibi, nōbīs) argentō
terms.comment: The everyday way to say “need”: mihi opus est librō or liber mihi opus est, I need a book; with a participle in the ablative, quid factō opus est?, what needs doing? (Lewis & Short, s.v. opus).
Of a person or a situation that asks for something.

terms.grammar: verb, second conjugation, with the ablative or the genitive
evidence: Cic. Lael. 17: egetque exercitātiōne nōn parvā

phrases.latin: Nunc hic diēs aliam vītam affert, aliōs mōrēs postulat.
phrases.english: Now this day brings a different life with it and calls for different ways.

phrases.latin: magnum opus est egetque exercitātiōne nōn parvā
phrases.english: it is a great task and needs no small practice

phrases.latin: Plūs scīs quid factō opus est.
phrases.english: You know better what needs to be done.
